title: The Risks of Downplaying China’s Military
gist: A CNAS commentary (excerpt) pushes back on the recurring argument—most recently from retired Adm. Dennis Blair in Foreign Affairs—that China's military threat to Taiwan is overstated, cataloguing concrete PLA build-up (modified civilian ferries, ship-to-shore equipment, hardened air bases, expanded missile forces) and arguing deterrence can still succeed if the US, Taiwan and allies invest with urgency.

insights.claim: China has spent years modifying civilian ferries to launch amphibious armored vehicles, developing equipment to move forces ashore without conventional ports, hardening dozens of air bases, and rapidly expanding missile forces that could deter or defeat a US intervention.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Concrete capabilities like ferry-launched amphibious assault and hardened bases signal a maturing invasion option—raising Taiwan-contingency tail risk for regional assets.
insights.quote: China has spent years modifying civilian ferries to launch amphibious armored vehicles, developing specialized equipment to move forces ashore without conventional port facilities, hardening dozens of air bases
insights.locator: This article was originally published in War on the Rocks.

insights.claim: A recurring line of analysis argues concerns about China's military capabilities are overstated and that an invasion of Taiwan remains beyond the reach of the People's Liberation Army.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The existence of a credible 'China can't invade' school is itself a market-relevant complacency risk the author warns against.
insights.quote: concerns about China’s military capabilities are overstated — and that an invasion of Taiwan remains beyond the reach of the People’s Liberation Army
insights.locator: Yet at the same time, a recurring line of analysis

insights.claim: Skeptics of the China threat variously cite the PLA's political character, lack of combat experience, institutional shortcomings, the extraordinary obstacles an invasion would face, and purges signaling internal dysfunction; retired Adm. Dennis Blair argued in Foreign Affairs that China cannot conquer Taiwan and is unlikely to become capable soon.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Naming Blair's Foreign Affairs argument pinpoints the specific optimistic case investors and policymakers may be anchoring on—worth weighing against the build-up evidence.
insights.quote: Adm. (ret.) Dennis Blair argued in Foreign Affairs that China cannot conquer Taiwan and is unlikely to become capable of doing so anytime soon.

insights.claim: CNAS argues deterrence can succeed and that continued US, Taiwanese and allied investment can matter a great deal—if undertaken with the urgency the situation demands.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The 'invest with urgency' framing supports sustained defense spending toward Taiwan deterrence—a tailwind for allied defense procurement.
insights.quote: Deterrence can succeed, and continued U.S., Taiwanese, and allied investment can matter a great deal — if undertaken with the urgency the situation demands.
